486. Declaration by sureties.—Every person standing surety to an accused person for his release on 
bail, shall make a declaration before the Court as to the number of persons to whom he has stood surety 
including the accused, giving therein all the relevant particulars. 
487. Discharge from custody.—(1) As soon as the bond or bail bond has been executed, the person 
for whose appearance it has been executed shall be released; and, when he is in jail, the court admitting him 
to bail shall issue an order of release to the officer in charge of the jail, and such officer on receipt of the 
orders shall release him. 
(2) Nothing in this section, section 478 or section 480, shall be deemed to require the release of any 
person liable to be detained for some matter other than that in respect of which the bond or bail bond was 
executed. 
488. Power to order sufficient bail when that first taken is insufficient.—If, through mistake, 
fraud or otherwise, insufficient sureties have been accepted, or if they afterwards become insufficient, the 
Court may issue a warrant of arrest directing that the person released on bail be brought before it and may 
order him to find sufficient sureties, and, on his failing so to do, may commit him to jail. 
489. Discharge of sureties.—(1) All or any sureties for the attendance and appearance of a person 
released on bail may at any time apply to a Magistrate to discharge the bond, either wholly or so far as 
relates to the applicants. 
(2) On such application being made, the Magistrate shall issue his warrant of arrest directing that the 
person so released be brought before him. 
(3) On the appearance of such person pursuant to the warrant, or on his voluntary surrender, the 
Magistrate shall direct the bond to be discharged either wholly or so far as relates to the applicants, and 
shall call upon such person to find other sufficient sureties, and, if he fails to do so, may commit him to jail. 
490. Deposit instead of recognizance.—When any person is required by any Court or officer to 
execute a bond or bail bond, such Court or officer may, except in the case of a bond for good behaviour, 
permit him to deposit a sum of money or Government promissory notes to such amount as the Court or 
officer may fix in lieu of executing such bond.  
491. Procedure when bond has been forfeited.—(1) Where, — 
(a) a bond under this Sanhita is for appearance, or for production of property, before a Court and it 
is proved to the satisfaction of that Court, or of any Court to which the case has subsequently been 
transferred, that the bond has been forfeited; or 
(b) in respect of any other bond under this Sanhita, it is proved to the satisfaction of the Court by 
which the bond was taken, or of any Court to which the case has subsequently been transferred, or of 
the Court of any Magistrate of the first class, that the bond has been forfeited,  
the Court shall record the grounds of such proof, and may call upon any person bound by such bond to pay 
the penalty thereof or to show cause why it should not be paid. 
Explanation.—A condition in a bond for appearance, or for production of property, before a Court shall 
be construed as including a condition for appearance, or as the case may be, for production of property, 
before any Court to which the case may subsequently be transferred. 
(2) If sufficient cause is not shown and the penalty is not paid, the Court may proceed to recover the 
same as if such penalty were a fine imposed by it under this Sanhita: 
Provided that where such penalty is not paid and cannot be recovered in the manner aforesaid, the 
person so bound as surety shall be liable, by order of the Court ordering the recovery of the penalty, to 
imprisonment in civil jail for a term which may extend to six months.

The partial document outlines various legal provisions related to bail and surety in criminal proceedings. Key points include:

1. **Declaration by Sureties**: Individuals providing surety for an accused must declare the number of persons they have stood surety for, including the accused.

2. **Discharge from Custody**: Upon execution of a bail bond, the accused must be released from custody, with specific provisions for those detained for other matters.

3. **Insufficient Sureties**: The court has the authority to demand sufficient sureties if the initially accepted ones are found to be inadequate.

4. **Discharge of Sureties**: Sureties can apply to a Magistrate to be discharged from their obligations, leading to potential re-evaluation of the bond.

5. **Deposit Instead of Recognizance**: Courts may allow a monetary deposit in lieu of executing a bond, except in specific cases.

6. **Bond Forfeiture Procedure**: The document details the process for handling forfeited bonds, including penalties and the potential for imprisonment if conditions are not met.

7. **Cancellation of Bonds**: Provisions for the cancellation of bonds upon breach of conditions are outlined, including the inability to release the accused solely on their bond.

8. **Insolvency or Death of Surety**: Procedures are established for when a surety becomes insolvent or dies, requiring fresh security.

9. **Child Bonds**: Special provisions for bonds required from minors are mentioned.

10. **Appeals**: Orders related to bond forfeiture are appealable to higher courts.

11. **Property Disposal**: The document concludes with provisions for the custody and disposal of property pending trial.

497. Order for custody and disposal of property pending trial in certain cases.—(1) When any 
property is produced before any Criminal Court or the Magistrate empowered to take cognizance or commit

or trial, and, if the property is subject to speedy and natural decay, or if it is otherwise expedient so to do, 
the Court or the Magistrate may, after recording such evidence as it thinks necessary, order it to be sold or 
otherwise disposed of. 
Explanation.—For the purposes of this section, “property” includes— 
(a) property of any kind or document which is produced before the Court or which is in its custody; 
(b) any property regarding which an offence appears to have been committed or which appears to 
have been used for the commission of any offence. 
(2) The Court or the Magistrate shall, within a period of fourteen days from the production of the 
property referred to in sub-section (1) before it, prepare a statement of such property containing its 
description in such form and manner as the State Government may, by rules, provide. 
(3) The Court or the Magistrate shall cause to be taken the photograph and if necessary, videograph on 
mobile phone or any electronic media, of the property referred to in sub-section (1). 
(4) The statement prepared under sub-section (2) and the photograph or the videography taken under 
sub-section (3) shall be used as evidence in any inquiry, trial or other proceeding under the Sanhita. 
(5) The Court or the Magistrate shall, within a period of thirty days after the statement has been prepared 
under sub-section (2) and the photograph or the videography has been taken under sub-section (3), order 
the disposal, destruction, confiscation or delivery of the property in the manner specified hereinafter. 
498. Order for disposal of property at conclusion of trial.—(1) When an investigation, inquiry or 
trial in any criminal case is concluded, the Court or the Magistrate may make such order as it thinks fit for 
the disposal, by destruction, confiscation or delivery to any person claiming to be entitled to possession 
thereof or otherwise, of any property or document produced before it or in its custody, or regarding which 
any offence appears to have been committed, or which has been used for the commission of any offence. 
(2) An order may be made under sub-section (1) for the delivery of any property to any person claiming 
to be entitled to the possession thereof, without any condition or on condition that he executes a bond, with 
or without securities, to the satisfaction of the Court or the Magistrate, engaging to restore such property to 
the Court if the order made under sub-section (1) is modified or set aside on appeal or revision. 
(3) A Court of Session may, instead of itself making an order under sub-section (1), direct the property 
to be delivered to the Chief Judicial Magistrate, who shall thereupon deal with it in the manner provided in 
sections 503, 504 and 505. 
(4) Except where the property is livestock or is subject to speedy and natural decay, or where a bond 
has been executed in pursuance of sub-section (2), an order made under sub-section (1) shall not be carried 
out for two months, or when an appeal is presented, until such appeal has been disposed of. 
(5) In this section, the term “property” includes, in the case of property regarding which an offence 
appears to have been committed, not only such property as has been originally in the possession or under 
the control of any party, but also any property into or for which the same may have been converted or 
exchanged, and anything acquired by such conversion or exchange, whether immediately or otherwise. 
499. Payment to innocent purchaser of money found on accused.—When any person is convicted 
of any offence which includes, or amounts to, theft or receiving stolen property, and it is proved that any 
other person bought the stolen property from him without knowing or having reason to believe that the 
same was stolen, and that any money has on his arrest been taken out of the possession of the convicted 
person, the Court may, on the application of such purchaser and on the restitution of the stolen property to 
the person entitled to the possession thereof, order that out of such money a sum not exceeding the price 
paid by such purchaser be delivered to him within six months from the date of such order.

500. Appeal against orders under section 498 or section 499.—(1) Any person aggrieved by an order 
made by a Court or Magistrate under section 498 or section 499, may appeal against it to the Court to which 
appeals ordinarily lie from convictions by the former Court. 
(2) On such appeal, the Appellate Court may direct the order to be stayed pending disposal of the 
appeal, or may modify, alter or annul the order and make any further orders that may be just. 
(3) The powers referred to in sub-section (2) may also be exercised by a Court of appeal, confirmation 
or revision while dealing with the case in which the order referred to in sub-section (1) was made. 
501. Destruction of libellous and other matter.—(1) On a conviction under section 294, section 295, 
or sub-sections (3) and (4) of section 356 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, the Court may order the 
destruction of all the copies of the thing in respect of which the conviction was had, and which are in the 
custody of the Court or remain in the possession or power of the person convicted. 
(2) The Court may, in like manner, on a conviction under section 274, section 275, section 276 
or section 277 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, order the food, drink, drug or medical preparation in 
respect of which the conviction was had, to be destroyed. 
502. Power to restore possession of immovable property.—(1) When a person is convicted of an 
offence by use of criminal force or show of force or by criminal intimidation, and it appears to the Court 
that, by such use of force or show of force or intimidation, any person has been dispossessed of any 
immovable property, the Court may, if it thinks fit, order that possession of the same be restored to that 
person after evicting by force, if necessary, any other person who may be in possession of the property: 
Provided that no such order shall be made by the Court more than one month after the date of the 
conviction. 
(2) Where the Court trying the offence has not made an order under sub-section (1), the Court of appeal, 
confirmation or revision may, if it thinks fit, make such order while disposing of the appeal, reference or 
revision, as the case may be. 
(3) Where an order has been made under sub-section (1), the provisions of section 500 shall apply in 
relation thereto as they apply in relation to an order under section 499. 
(4) No order made under this section shall prejudice any right or interest to or in such immovable 
property which any person may be able to establish in a civil suit. 
503. Procedure by police upon seizure of property.—(1) Whenever the seizure of property by any 
police officer is reported to a Magistrate under the provisions of this Sanhita, and such property is not 
produced before a Criminal Court during an inquiry or trial, the Magistrate may make such order as he 
thinks fit respecting the disposal of such property or the delivery of such property to the person entitled to 
the possession thereof, or if such person cannot be ascertained, respecting the custody and production of 
such property. 
(2) If the person so entitled is known, the Magistrate may order the property to be delivered to him on 
such conditions (if any) as the Magistrate thinks fit and if such person is unknown, the Magistrate may 
detain it and shall, in such case, issue a proclamation specifying the articles of which such property consists, 
and requiring any person who may have a claim thereto, to appear before him and establish his claim within 
six months from the date of such proclamation. 
504. Procedure where no claimant appears within six months.—(1) If no person within such period 
establishes his claim to such property, and if the person in whose possession such property was found is 
unable to show that it was legally acquired by him, the Magistrate may by order direct that such property 
shall be at the disposal of the State Government and may be sold by that Government and the proceeds of 
such sale shall be dealt with in such manner as the State Government may, by rules, provide.

3. **Irregular Proceedings**: It distinguishes between irregularities that do not invalidate proceedings and those that do. 6. **Effect of Errors in Charges**: It clarifies that findings or sentences are not invalidated due to errors or omissions in charges unless they cause a failure of justice, and outlines the procedures for addressing such issues.

7. **Reversibility of Findings or Sentences**: It emphasizes that courts should not reverse or alter findings or sentences due to procedural errors unless a failure of justice is evident, taking into account whether objections were raised timely.

Overall, the document addresses the procedural integrity of criminal proceedings and the conditions under which irregularities may affect the validity of judicial actions.

2. **Proceedings in Wrong Place**: A court's finding or sentence cannot be invalidated solely due to the proceedings occurring in an incorrect jurisdiction unless it results in a failure of justice.

3. **Non-compliance with Recording Provisions**: Courts can admit confessions or statements even if there was non-compliance with specific recording provisions, provided it did not harm the accused's defense.

4. **Charge Errors**: Findings or sentences are not invalidated due to errors or omissions in charges unless they cause a failure of justice. Courts can order a new trial or frame charges if necessary.

5. **Reversibility of Findings**: Courts of appeal cannot reverse findings based on procedural errors unless a failure of justice is established.

6. **Attachment Validity**: Attachments made under the law are not deemed unlawful due to defects in the related documents.

7. **Limitation Periods**: The document specifies limitation periods for taking cognizance of offenses, detailing different durations based on the severity of the offense.

8. **Commencement of Limitation**: The limitation period begins from the date of the offense or when the offense becomes known to the aggrieved party or police.

9. **Exclusion of Time**: Certain periods, such as ongoing prosecutions or injunctions, are excluded from the limitation period calculation.

Overall, the document emphasizes the importance of procedural integrity while also providing mechanisms to address errors without compromising justice.

520. Trials before High Courts.—When an offence is tried by the High Court otherwise than under 
section 447, it shall, in the trial of the offence, observe the same procedure as a Court of Sessions would

Central Government may make rules consistent with this Sanhita and the Air Force Act, 1950 (45 of 1950),

from any judgment or order passed or made by himself.

any case by reason only that he is concerned therein in a public capacity, or by reason only that he has

(c) any sanction accorded or consent given under the said Code in pursuance of which no 
proceeding was commenced under that Code, shall be deemed to have been accorded or given under 
the corresponding provisions of this Sanhita and proceedings may be commenced under this Sanhita in 
pursuance of such sanction or consent. 
(3) Where the period specified for an application or other proceeding under the said Code had expired 
on or before the commencement of this Sanhita, nothing in this Sanhita shall be construed as enabling any 
such application to be made or proceeding to be commenced under this Sanhita by reason only of the fact 
that a longer period therefor is specified by this Sanhita or provisions are made in this Sanhita for the 
extension of time.

Refusing oath when duly required to take oath by a public servant.
nodes.summary: The partial document outlines various legal offenses related to the refusal to cooperate with public servants and the provision of false information. It details specific actions, such as refusing to take an oath, refusing to answer questions, and refusing to sign statements when legally required, along with the corresponding penalties, which include simple imprisonment, fines, or both. The offenses are categorized as non-cognizable and bailable, with jurisdiction specified for the courts where these offenses are committed. Additionally, the document addresses more serious offenses, such as knowingly providing false information under oath and giving false information to public servants, along with their respective penalties. Overall, the document emphasizes the legal obligations of individuals to cooperate with public authorities and the consequences of failing to do so.

nodes.title: Obstructing sale of property offered for sale by authority of a public servant.
nodes.summary:
The partial document outlines various legal offenses related to obstructing or interfering with the duties of public servants, along with the corresponding penalties. Key points include:

1. **Obstruction of Sale**: Offenses related to obstructing the sale of property by a public servant, with penalties of imprisonment or fines.
2. **Illegal Purchase/Bid**: Penalties for illegal purchases or bids on property offered for sale by public servants.
3. **Obstruction of Public Functions**: Offenses for obstructing public servants in their duties, with varying imprisonment terms and fines.
4. **Failure to Assist**: Legal consequences for failing to assist public servants when required by law.
5. **Disobedience to Orders**: Penalties for disobeying lawful orders from public servants, especially if it causes harm or danger.
6. **Threats Against Public Servants**: Offenses related to threatening public servants or inducing others to refrain from seeking their protection.
7. **False Evidence**: Severe penalties for intentionally providing false evidence in judicial proceedings.

The document specifies the nature of each offense, the type of punishment (imprisonment, fines, or both), and the jurisdiction of any magistrate to handle these cases.

nodes.title: Intentionally giving or fabricating false evidence in a judicial proceeding.
nodes.summary:
The partial document outlines various legal offenses related to obstructing public servants and providing false evidence in judicial proceedings. It specifies the penalties for each offense, including imprisonment terms, fines, and whether the offenses are cognizable or non-cognizable, bailable or non-bailable. Key points include:

1. **Obstruction of Public Servants**: Offenses such as obstructing the sale of property, illegal purchases, and failing to assist public servants are detailed, with varying penalties from fines to imprisonment.

2. **Disobedience to Orders**: Disobedience to lawful orders from public servants is categorized based on the severity of the consequences, with harsher penalties for actions that endanger life or public safety.

3. **Threats Against Public Servants**: Threatening public servants or inducing individuals to refrain from seeking protection is addressed, with specified imprisonment terms.

4. **False Evidence**: Multiple offenses related to giving or fabricating false evidence are outlined, including severe penalties for those leading to wrongful convictions, especially in capital cases.

5. **Certificates and Declarations**: Offenses involving the issuance of false certificates and making false statements in legal declarations are also covered, with penalties aligned with those for giving false evidence.

Overall, the document serves as a legal framework for addressing offenses against public servants and the integrity of judicial processes.

It details the penalties associated with different scenarios, including imprisonment terms, fines, and the nature of the offenses (cognizable or non-cognizable, bailable or non-bailable). Key points include:

1. **False Evidence**: Different sections specify penalties for giving or fabricating false evidence, with harsher penalties for cases intended to cause wrongful convictions, especially in capital offenses.
2. **Threatening for False Evidence**: There are provisions for threatening individuals to provide false evidence, with corresponding penalties.
3. **Use of False Evidence**: The document addresses the use of evidence known to be false in judicial proceedings and the consequences of issuing or signing false certificates.
4. **Consequences of Wrongful Conviction**: It highlights severe penalties if an innocent person is convicted based on false evidence, including potential death sentences.
5. **Jurisdiction**: It specifies the courts that have jurisdiction over these offenses, indicating whether they are triable in a Magistrate's court or a Court of Session. 

Overall, the document serves as a legal framework for addressing and penalizing the act of providing false evidence in judicial settings.

nodes.summary:
The partial document outlines various legal provisions related to the offense of giving or fabricating false evidence. It specifies the penalties associated with different scenarios, including imprisonment terms, fines, and the nature of the offenses (cognizable or non-cognizable, bailable or non-bailable). Key points include:

1. **False Evidence**: Different sections detail penalties for giving or fabricating false evidence, with severe consequences for cases intended to cause wrongful convictions, especially in capital offenses.
2. **Threatening for False Evidence**: There are provisions for threatening individuals to provide false evidence, with penalties that escalate if an innocent person is convicted as a result.
3. **Use of False Evidence in Judicial Proceedings**: The document addresses the use of known false evidence in court, along with penalties similar to those for giving false evidence.
4. **False Certificates and Statements**: It includes offenses related to issuing false certificates and making false statements in declarations that are legally admissible as evidence, with corresponding penalties.

Overall, the document emphasizes the seriousness of false evidence in legal proceedings and outlines the legal repercussions for such actions.

nodes.summary:
The partial document outlines various legal offenses related to false evidence and obstruction of justice, detailing the nature of each offense, the corresponding penalties, and the jurisdictional authority for prosecution. Key points include:

1. **False Evidence**: Offenses related to giving false evidence are categorized as non-cognizable and bailable, with specific courts designated for trial.
2. **Disappearance of Evidence**: Different penalties are prescribed based on the severity of the underlying offense, ranging from 3 years to 7 years of imprisonment, along with fines.
3. **Omission to Inform**: Individuals legally required to report offenses but fail to do so face penalties of up to 6 months imprisonment or fines.
4. **False Information**: Providing false information about an offense can result in up to 2 years of imprisonment or fines.
5. **Destruction of Evidence**: Secreting or destroying documents to prevent their use as evidence carries a penalty of up to 3 years imprisonment.
6. **False Personation**: Engaging in false personation for legal proceedings or bail purposes is punishable by up to 3 years imprisonment.
7. **Fraudulent Property Concealment**: Concealing property to evade legal consequences can lead to similar penalties as other offenses listed.

Overall, the document emphasizes the legal repercussions for actions that undermine the integrity of the judicial process.

nodes.title: Criminal proceeding instituted on a false charge of an offence punishable with death, imprisonment for life, or imprisonment for ten years or upwards.
nodes.summary:
The partial document outlines various legal offenses related to fraud and deception, along with their corresponding penalties. Key points include:

1. **Claiming Property Without Right**: Offenders can face up to 2 years of imprisonment or a fine for falsely claiming property to avoid forfeiture or fines.
2. **Fraudulent Decrees**: Several sections address the consequences of fraudulently allowing decrees to pass or be executed for sums not due, with penalties of up to 2 years of imprisonment or fines.
3. **False Claims in Court**: Making false claims in court can result in 2 years of imprisonment and fines.
4. **False Charges**: There are severe penalties for making false charges intended to injure others, with imprisonment up to 5 years or fines, and even harsher penalties for false charges related to serious offenses.
5. **Harboring Offenders**: The document specifies penalties for harboring offenders based on the severity of the original offense, ranging from 3 years to 5 years of imprisonment, depending on the nature of the crime.

All offenses listed are categorized as non-cognizable or cognizable, with bailable options available, and the authority of the magistrate or court specified for each case.

nodes.summary:
The partial document outlines various legal offenses related to fraud and deception, along with their corresponding penalties. Key points include:

1. **Claiming Property Without Right (Section 244)**: Punishable by up to 2 years of imprisonment or a fine, or both. It is non-cognizable and bailable, handled by any Magistrate.

2. **Fraudulent Decree (Section 245)**: Involves allowing a decree to pass for an incorrect sum or executing a satisfied decree, with similar penalties as above, but specifically requires a first-class Magistrate.

3. **False Claims in Court (Section 246)**: Punishable by 2 years of imprisonment and a fine, also non-cognizable and bailable, overseen by a first-class Magistrate.

4. **Fraudulent Decree Execution (Section 247)**: Similar to Section 245, it addresses obtaining a decree for an incorrect sum or executing a satisfied decree, with the same penalties.

5. **False Charges (Section 248)**: Includes false charges made with intent to harm, punishable by up to 5 years or a fine of 2 lakh rupees. A more severe penalty applies for false charges related to serious offenses, with imprisonment of up to 10 years.

6. **Harboring Offenders (Sections 249)**: Different penalties based on the severity of the original offense, ranging from 3 years for harboring offenders of serious crimes to lesser penalties for minor offenses, all of which are cognizable and bailable, managed by a first-class Magistrate. 

Overall, the document details the legal repercussions for various fraudulent activities and false accusations, emphasizing the seriousness of such offenses in the legal system.

nodes.title: Taking gift to help to recover movable property of which a person has been deprived by an offence without causing apprehension of offender.
nodes.summary:
The partial document outlines various legal provisions related to the punishment for offenses involving the screening of offenders from punishment, offering gifts or restoration of property, and harboring offenders. It specifies the penalties based on the severity of the offense, categorizing them into three main sections: 

1. **Taking Gifts to Screen Offenders**: 
   - For offenses punishable by death, the penalty is 7 years of imprisonment and a fine.
   - For life imprisonment or 10-year offenses, the penalty is 3 years of imprisonment and a fine.
   - For offenses punishable by less than 10 years, the penalty is one-fourth of the longest term or a fine, or both.

2. **Offering Gifts or Restoration of Property**: 
   - Similar penalties apply as in the first section, with distinctions made for cognizable and non-cognizable offenses.

3. **Harboring Offenders**: 
   - The penalties for harboring offenders vary based on the severity of the original offense, with imprisonment terms ranging from 3 years to 7 years, depending on whether the offense is punishable by death, life imprisonment, or less than 10 years.

All offenses are categorized as cognizable or non-cognizable and are bailable, with jurisdiction specified for a Magistrate of the first class.

nodes.title: Omission to apprehend, or sufferance of escape on part of public servant, in cases not otherwise provided for: --
nodes.summary:
The partial document outlines various legal offenses and their corresponding penalties, focusing on actions related to public servants, judicial proceedings, and public health. Key points include:

1. **Omission to Apprehend**: Differentiates between intentional and negligent omissions by public servants, with penalties ranging from 2 to 3 years of imprisonment or fines.
2. **Resistance to Apprehension**: Addresses penalties for obstructing lawful apprehension, with a maximum of 6 months imprisonment.
3. **Violation of Remission Conditions**: Discusses consequences for violating conditions of punishment remission, leading to reinstatement of original sentences.
4. **Insulting Public Servants**: Outlines penalties for intentional insults to public servants during judicial proceedings, with fines and imprisonment.
5. **Personation of Assessors**: Specifies penalties for impersonating an assessor, including imprisonment for up to 2 years.
6. **Failure to Appear in Court**: Details penalties for individuals released on bail who fail to appear, with a maximum of 1 year imprisonment.
7. **Spreading Infection**: Differentiates between negligent and malignant actions that could spread dangerous diseases, with penalties ranging from 6 months to 2 years.
8. **Disobeying Quarantine Rules**: Addresses penalties for knowingly disobeying quarantine regulations.
9. **Food Adulteration**: Discusses penalties for adulterating food or drink intended for sale, with fines and imprisonment.

The document categorizes offenses as cognizable or non-cognizable and specifies the type of magistrate that can adjudicate each case.

nodes.title: Negligent conduct with respect to pulling down, repairing or constructing buildings, etc.
nodes.summary:
The partial document outlines various legal offenses and their corresponding penalties, focusing on negligent conduct, public nuisance, obscenity, lottery-related activities, and religious offenses. Key points include:

1. **Negligent Conduct**: Offenses related to building construction and animal care carry penalties of up to 6 months imprisonment or fines of 5,000 rupees, with varying cognizability and bail status.
2. **Public Nuisance**: Committing public nuisance can result in fines, while continuing a nuisance after an injunction can lead to imprisonment or fines.
3. **Obscenity**: Selling obscene materials, especially to minors, incurs significant penalties, including imprisonment and fines that increase with repeat offenses.
4. **Lottery Offenses**: Keeping a lottery office or publishing lottery proposals is punishable by fines or imprisonment, depending on the specific offense.
5. **Religious Offenses**: Defiling a place of worship with intent to insult a religion can lead to imprisonment for up to 2 years and is non-bailable.

Overall, the document serves as a legal reference for various offenses, their classifications, and the judicial authority involved in adjudicating these matters.

nodes.title: Belonging to a gang of persons associated for the purpose of habitually committing dacoity.
nodes.summary:
The partial document outlines various criminal offenses related to robbery, dacoity, theft, and misappropriation of property, along with their corresponding penalties and legal classifications. Key points include:

1. **Gang-related Offenses**: Membership in a gang for committing dacoity is punishable by life imprisonment or a minimum of 10 years, categorized as cognizable and non-bailable, tried in a Court of Session.

2. **Robbery and Dacoity**: Attempting robbery or dacoity with intent to cause death or serious injury carries a minimum sentence of 7 years, also cognizable and non-bailable.

3. **Use of Deadly Weapons**: Attempting robbery or dacoity while armed results in a minimum of 7 years imprisonment, similarly classified.

4. **Wandering Gangs**: Belonging to a wandering gang for habitual thefts incurs a 7-year rigorous imprisonment, cognizable and non-bailable, tried in a first-class Magistrate's court.

5. **Misappropriation of Property**: Dishonest misappropriation of movable property can lead to 6 months to 2 years imprisonment, non-cognizable and bailable.

6. **Property of Deceased Persons**: Misappropriation of property from a deceased person carries a 3-year sentence, with harsher penalties for clerks or employees of the deceased.

7. **Criminal Breach of Trust**: Various forms of criminal breach of trust are detailed, with penalties ranging from 5 years to life imprisonment, depending on the offender's role (e.g., public servant, banker).

8. **Receiving Stolen Property**: Dishonestly receiving stolen property is punishable by up to 3 years imprisonment, cognizable and non-bailable.

Overall, the document serves as a legal reference for the classification of crimes, their penalties, and the judicial processes involved.

nodes.summary: The partial document outlines the classification of offences under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, providing a detailed schedule that includes various offences, their corresponding punishments, and whether they are cognizable or non-cognizable, bailable or non-bailable. It begins with explanatory notes clarifying terms such as "Magistrate of the first class" and the definitions of cognizable and non-cognizable offences. The document lists specific offences related to abetment, rape, sexual harassment, and other crimes, detailing the penalties associated with each offence, including imprisonment terms and fines. It also specifies the courts that have jurisdiction over these offences, emphasizing the legal framework for addressing various criminal acts in India.

nodes.summary: The partial document outlines key provisions related to the administration of justice under a new legal framework. It emphasizes the High Court's responsibility to oversee the efficient functioning of subordinate courts, ensuring timely case resolutions. It introduces the possibility of conducting trials and proceedings electronically, covering various aspects such as summons issuance, witness examination, and evidence recording. Additionally, it details the repeal of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, while providing transitional provisions to handle ongoing cases and legal actions under the previous code until the new framework is fully implemented. The document also clarifies that certain existing legal notifications and sanctions will continue to be recognized under the new system.
nodes.text:
172 
 
529. Duty of High Court to exercise continuous superintendence over Courts.—Every High Court 
shall so exercise its superintendence over the Courts of Session and Courts of Judicial Magistrates 
subordinate to it as to ensure that there is an expeditious and proper disposal of cases by the Judges and 
Magistrates. 
530. Trial and proceedings to be held in electronic mode.—All trials, inquires and proceedings under 
this Sanhita, including— 
(i) issuance, service and execution of summons and warrant; 
(ii) examination of complainant and witnesses; 
(iii) recording of evidence in inquiries and trials; and 
(iv) all appellate proceedings or any other proceeding,  
may be held in electronic mode, by use of electronic communication or use of audio-video electronic means. 
531. Repeal and savings.—(1) The Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (2 of 1974) is hereby repealed. 
(2) Notwithstanding such repeal— 
(a) if, immediately before the date on which this Sanhita comes into force, there is any appeal, 
application, trial, inquiry or investigation pending, then, such appeal, application, trial, inquiry or 
investigation shall be disposed of, continued, held or made, as the case may be, in accordance with the 
provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (2 of 1974), as in force immediately before such 
commencement (hereinafter referred to as the said Code), as if this Sanhita had not come into force; 
(b) all notifications published, proclamations issued, powers conferred, forms provided by rules, 
local jurisdictions defined, sentences passed and orders, rules and appointments, not being 
appointments as Special Magistrates, made under the said Code and which are in force immediately 
before the commencement of this Sanhita, shall be deemed, respectively, to have been published, 
issued, conferred, specified, defined, passed or made under the corresponding provisions of this 
Sanhita; 
(c) any sanction accorded or consent given under the said Code in pursuance of which no 
proceeding was commenced under that Code, shall be deemed to have been accorded or given under 
the corresponding provisions of this Sanhita and proceedings may be commenced under this Sanhita in 
pursuance of such sanction or consent. 
(3) Where the period specified for an application or other proceeding under the said Code had expired 
on or before the commencement of this Sanhita, nothing in this Sanhita shall be construed as enabling any 
such application to be made or proceeding to be commenced under this Sanhita by reason only of the fact 
that a longer period therefor is specified by this Sanhita or provisions are made in this Sanhita for the 
extension of time.

structure.summary: The partial document outlines the legal provisions regarding the suspension, remission, and commutation of sentences. It specifies that conditions for sentence suspension may depend on the individual or be independent of their will. The document details the requirements for presenting petitions for sentence suspension, particularly emphasizing that such petitions will only be considered if the sentenced individual is incarcerated. It defines the "appropriate Government" responsible for these actions, distinguishing between the Central Government and State Government based on the nature of the offence. Additionally, it grants the appropriate Government the authority to commute various types of sentences without the consent of the sentenced individual, while also imposing restrictions on remission or commutation in certain serious cases, particularly those involving life sentences or death sentences. Lastly, it notes that the Central Government can exercise powers related to death sentences, and that State Governments must coordinate with the Central Government in specific cases.

fulfilled by the person in whose favour the sentence is suspended or remitted, or one independent of his 
will. 
(5) The appropriate Government may, by general rules or special orders, give directions as to the 
suspension of sentences and the conditions on which petitions should be presented and dealt with: 
Provided that in the case of any sentence (other than a sentence of fine) passed on a person above the 
age of eighteen years, no such petition by the person sentenced or by any other person on his behalf shall 
be entertained, unless the person sentenced is in jail, and— 
(a) where such petition is made by the person sentenced, it is presented through the officer in charge 
of the jail; or 
(b) where such petition is made by any other person, it contains a declaration that the person 
sentenced is in jail. 
(6) The provisions of the above sub-sections shall also apply to any order passed by a Criminal Court 
under any section of this Sanhita or of any other law, which restricts the liberty of any person or imposes 
any liability upon him or his property. 
(7) In this section and in section 474, the expression “appropriate Government” means,— 
(a) in cases where the sentence is for an offence against, or the order referred to in sub-section (6) 
is passed under, any law relating to a matter to which the executive power of the Union extends, the 
Central Government; 
(b) in other cases, the Government of the State within which the offender is sentenced or the said 
order is passed. 
474. Power to commute sentence.—The appropriate Government may, without the consent of the 
person sentenced, commute— 
(a) a sentence of death, for imprisonment for life; 
(b) a sentence of imprisonment for life, for imprisonment for a term not less than seven years; 
(c) a sentence of imprisonment for seven years or more, for imprisonment for a term not less than 
three years; 
(d) a sentence of imprisonment for less than seven years, for fine; 
(e) a sentence of rigorous imprisonment, for simple imprisonment for any term to which that person 
might have been sentenced. 
475. Restriction on powers of remission or commutation in certain cases.—Notwithstanding 
anything contained in section 473, where a sentence of imprisonment for life is imposed on conviction of a 
person for an offence for which death is one of the punishments provided by law, or where a sentence of 
death imposed on a person has been commuted under section 474 into one of imprisonment for life, such 
person shall not be released from prison unless he had served at least fourteen years of imprisonment.

by sections 473 and 474 upon the State Government may, in the case of sentences of death, also be exercised
